name: Left-Digit Effect
description: People judge the difference between numbers by their leftmost digit, so $2.99 feels meaningfully cheaper than $3.00 even though the gap is one cent. It appears with prices and with other multidigit numbers.
design_relevance_note: The basis of 99-ending prices and a reason to check how thresholds (price points, odometer or rating cut-offs) are displayed.
myth_risk_note: Well supported, but its strength depends on how prices are presented; avoid quoting a single universal size.
prevalence_note: Standard in pricing practice and widely documented.

findings.description: Across five experiments, a nine-ending price is perceived as smaller than a price one cent higher only when the leftmost digits differ (e.g. $2.99 vs $3.00); the effect is stronger the closer the two compared prices are, and it also shows up with multidigit numbers that are not prices.
findings.source_title: Penny Wise and Pound Foolish: The Left‐Digit Effect in Price Cognition

findings.description: Across six studies (five experiments and a scanner panel study), left-digit bias is stronger when a focal price and reference price are seen side by side (stimulus-based evaluation) than when one must be retrieved from memory, where people more often round prices.
findings.source_title: The Left-Digit Bias: When and Why Are Consumers Penny Wise and Pound Foolish?

findings.description: In over 22 million wholesale used-car transactions, sale prices fall discontinuously at 10,000-mile odometer thresholds (and by less at 1,000-mile thresholds), evidence of left-digit bias in how odometer values are processed, even in a market with large stakes and easily observed information; the authors' evidence points to final customers rather than professional agents.
findings.effect_size: discontinuous price drops at 10,000-mile odometer thresholds; 22 million transactions
findings.source_title: Heuristic Thinking and Limited Attention in the Car Market

findings.description: In retail scanner data on 3,500 products from 25 U.S. chains, consumers respond to a one-cent increase from a ninety-nine-ending price as if it were more than a twenty-cent increase; retailers all use ninety-nine-ending prices but price as if the bias were much smaller than it is, forgoing an estimated 1-4% of potential gross profits.
findings.effect_size: a one-cent rise from a 99-ending price is treated as more than a 20-cent rise; retailers forgo 1-4% of potential gross profits
findings.source_title: More Than a Penny’s Worth: Left-Digit Bias and Firm Pricing
